meanings.note: Conversational pivot word acknowledging what was said before moving on or softening an apology.

examples.trans: Alright, what's the plan now?
Okay sorry, don't be upset.

meanings.note: Independent first-person singular pronoun for any gender.

examples.trans: I am a student at the school.
I didn't say anything.

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').

examples.trans: What are you doing here?
So, ready to go?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?
I didn't do anything wrong.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative base taking pronoun endings: إلي (to me), إلك (to you), إلها (to her), إلنا (for us), إلهم (to them).

examples.trans: This book is for you.
Tell me the truth.

meanings.note: Negates nouns, adjectives, participles, prepositional phrases, and لازم (مش صح، مش معنا، مش قادرة، مش بعد اليوم).

examples.trans: This talk is not true.
I'm not upset with you.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine manner word: ليش بتحكي هيك؟ ('why are you talking like that?'), زي هيك ('like this'), بعد هيك ('after this').

examples.trans: Don't talk to me like that.
That's not what we agreed on.

meanings.note: Used when reminding friends of what they agreed on (مش هيك الاتفاق 'that wasn't the deal').

examples.trans: That was our deal from the start.
We reached a clear agreement.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Spoken feminine singular 'you', spelled with final ي to reflect the Jordanian pronunciation inti.

examples.trans: Are you a new girl here?
What do you think?

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine counterpart of ظل; before another verb (يضل يتحمل، بتضلك تخططي) it means 'keep on doing'.

examples.trans: I stayed at school until afternoon.
You keep asking the same question.

meanings.note: Form II verb (khattat); بتضلك تخططي لحالك means 'you keep planning by yourself'.

examples.trans: We planned the trip together.
Why are you planning without us?

meanings.note: With suffixes, acts as the Levantine reflexive ('myself/themselves': حالهم), 'alone' (لحالك), and 'one's own business' (خليكم بحالكم).

examples.trans: I studied the lesson by myself.
Leave me to myself, please.

meanings.note: Refers to an account of events (القصة كلها) or informally to an ongoing drama (بالقصة).

examples.trans: Tell me the story from the beginning.
What's the story with the rooms on the trip?

meanings.note: The main Levantine verb for 'talk / say / tell', far more common in Amman than تكلم.

examples.trans: Who told you the news?
Tell me what happened with you.

meanings.note: Used before nouns (قبل بوقت 'ahead of time'), before ما + verb (قبل ما تعصب 'before she gets angry'), or alone at the end of a clause ('beforehand').

examples.trans: I arrived at school before the bell.
Tell me before you go.

meanings.note: Versatile noun: ما عندي وقت ('no time'), صار الوقت ('it's time'), وقتها ('at that moment / then'), مش وقته ('not the time for it').

examples.trans: I didn't have time to explain.
Everything is nice in its own time.

meanings.note: Followed by a noun or by ما + subjunctive verb (بدل ما أتفاجأ 'instead of my being surprised').

examples.text: تعالي معنا بدل ما تضلي لحالك.
examples.trans: Come with us instead of staying alone.
I had tea instead of coffee.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: Expresses being caught off guard (بدل ما أتفاجأ هيك 'instead of being surprised like this').

examples.trans: I was surprised when I saw you here.
Don't be surprised by the news.

meanings.note: Past tense linking verb (كنت، كنتي، كان، كنا) and subjunctive تكون / نكون ('to be'); ما كان عندي means 'I didn't have'.

examples.trans: I was at school in the morning.
Today was very long.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine form of يد. Idioms: بإيدي ('in my power/control') and إيد واحدة ('one hand' = united).

examples.trans: The matter wasn't in my hands.
We must stay united.

meanings.note: Form II transitive verb (ghayyar): أغير تقسيم الغرف ('change the room assignments').

examples.trans: I changed my mind about the matter.
Can we change our seats?

meanings.note: Verbal noun of قسم; تقسيم الغرف refers to the school-trip room assignments.

examples.trans: I didn't like the group assignments.
The room assignment list is ready.

meanings.note: Singular غرفة (الغرفة), plural غرف (تقسيم الغرف 'room assignments').

examples.trans: We are in the same room on the trip.
The room is neat and spacious.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word (pronounced ktiir) used before or after adjectives ('very') and after plural nouns ('many').

examples.trans: The movie was really good.
I have lots of friends at school.

meanings.note: Feminine متحمسة ('excited': كنت كتير متحمسة).

examples.trans: Dina is super excited for the trip.
We're all excited to see the movie.

meanings.note: Placed before a definite noun without changing form: بنفس الغرفة ('in the same room'), بنفس الوقت ('at the same time').

examples.trans: We ride the same bus.
We arrived at the same time.

meanings.note: Levantine 'want' built from بد- plus pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بدنا (we want).

examples.trans: What do you want to do now?
I wanted to talk with you.

meanings.note: In school speech, نقعد مع بعض means 'sit and hang out together'.

examples.trans: Come let's sit on the bench.
We hung out together at recess.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian pronoun corresponding to formal نحن.

examples.trans: We have been friends for a long time.
Come sit with us.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine pronunciation of ثلاثة; إحنا الثلاثة means 'the three of us'.

examples.trans: There are three of us in the same room.
I waited three minutes.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine adverb synonymous with مع بعض.

examples.trans: Let's sit together.
We went to the movie together.

meanings.note: Warm colloquial verb for casual, friendly chatting (ندردش طول الليل).

examples.trans: We sat chatting in the courtyard.
I love chatting with my friends.

meanings.note: Warm social verb for staying up at night talking with friends (نسهر طول الليل).

examples.trans: We stayed up until morning yesterday.
We love staying up and chatting together.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').

examples.trans: Come sit with us.
Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meanings.note: After مع, مع بعض means 'together / with one another'.

examples.trans: We walk home together.
We studied together yesterday.

meanings.note: Before a time noun (طول الليل 'all night long', طول اليوم 'all day'), expresses unbroken duration.

examples.trans: We studied together all day.
We stayed up all night.

meanings.note: طول الليل means 'all night long'.

examples.trans: We stayed up together all night.
It's quiet at night.

meanings.note: In the past مع ما (ما عرفت شو أعمل), means 'I didn't know what to do'; b-present بعرف means 'I know'.

examples.trans: I know this place well.
I didn't know how to answer the question.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also / too' (وأنا كمان 'and me too').

examples.trans: And my friends were there too.
I need five more minutes.

meanings.note: Active participle of حب used for polite wishes; with كنت (كنت حابة هيك) it means 'I would have loved that'.

examples.trans: I would have loved to sit with you.
I really like the idea.

meanings.note: Versatile Levantine word meaning 'but' between clauses and 'only / just' inside a clause.
As a focus adverb before a verb, noun, or imperative, بس narrows or softens the statement.

examples.trans: I tried to speak, but she didn't hear me.
I just want one minute.

meanings.note: With بـ, بصراحة means 'honestly / frankly'.

examples.trans: Honestly, I didn't feel comfortable about it.
Speak frankly with me.

meanings.note: Verbal noun: وجود نوف معهم ('Noaf's presence / having Noaf with them').

examples.trans: Having you with us makes us happy.
Thank you for being by my side.

meanings.note: وجود نوف معهم مفيد إلنا means 'Noaf's presence with them is helpful to us'.

examples.trans: This book is very useful.
Your advice was helpful to me.

meanings.note: Introduces conditions (لو ضلت معهم 'if she stays with them'), concessions (حتى لو 'even if'), and polite لو سمحتي ('please').

examples.trans: If I knew, I would have told you.
Help me, please.

meanings.note: Standard Levantine future marker placed before a bare subjunctive verb (رح أخلص، ما رح نسكت).

examples.trans: I'm going to tell the truth.
I won't forget this day.

meanings.note: Takes direct object suffixes (رح تساعدنا كتير 'she will help us a lot').

examples.trans: Could you help me a little?
Dina always helps her friends.

meanings.note: Used in the everyday imperative warning دير بالك / ديروا بالكم ('be careful / watch out').

examples.trans: Be careful on the road.
Watch out for them.

meanings.note: Core noun in the warning idiom دير بالك / ديروا بالكم ('take care / watch out').

examples.trans: Take care of yourself.
The matter didn't leave my mind.

meanings.note: Jordanian plural demonstrative for people: هدول البنات ('these/those girls').

examples.trans: Those girls are in our class.
Who are those people standing over there?

meanings.note: Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Plural طبيعيين ('normal people'); بشكل طبيعي means 'normally / casually'.

examples.trans: That is a very natural feeling.
I acted in a normal way.

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.
See you tomorrow morning!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'tomorrow' (أشوفك بكرة! 'See you tomorrow!').

examples.trans: We have an exam tomorrow morning.
See you tomorrow at school!
